submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective long-sentence wrap-up detector: activation is near zero through the first ~10 tokens after a sentence boundary and grows with how much of the current sentence has already been read (96% of its strongest activations sit >=15 tokens into a sentence; mean 0.16 of max past 20 tokens vs 0.02 before 15), so its peak is the token that closes a long, multi-clause sentence - a sentence-final '.' or ').' , a markup close such as ' </' - and secondarily a clause-separating comma/semicolon plus the first function word(s) of the clause it opens (' if', ' when', ' it', ' which', ' this', ' the', ' a', ' in', ' to'). It stays near zero on the first ~10 tokens of any sentence, on ordinary content words early in a sentence, and on commas inside enumerations, parentheticals, citations and dates (the negative pole is essentially silent, max 0.17 against 1.70 here).

We reached the harbour at dawn, before the cranes had started and before the fish market opened its shutters, and the only sound was slack rigging knocking against the masts of boats that had not yet left. My uncle had promised me a berth on a trawler bound for the northern banks, a promise he made every summer and broke every autumn, but this time he had actually spoken to the captain, and the captain had looked me over and said nothing at all.

The pier smelled of diesel and salt and old rope, the way it always did after a storm, and gulls stood on the pilings in a long grey row, watching us with the flat patience of creatures who have never once been hurried. I carried a canvas bag with two sweaters, a knife, a tin of biscuits and a letter from my mother that I had not opened, and I set it down beside a coil of orange rope while my uncle argued with a man about the price of ice.

The argument lasted longer than the loading, which is saying something, because loading a trawler involves hauling crates up a wet ramp for most of a morning. I stood near the rail and watched the town wake up behind us, the bakery lights coming on one window at a time, the priest crossing the square with his coat buttoned wrong, a dog trotting along the seawall as though it had somewhere important to be.

By the time we cast off the sun had climbed above the breakwater and the water had turned the colour of hammered tin, and I understood that I was finally leaving, that the years of promises had ended in this ordinary grey morning, and that nobody on the quay was waving. The engine settled into a slow rhythm that I would come to know better than my own heartbeat, a rhythm that made the deck plates hum and the cups rattle in their rack, and the harbour slid backwards until it was only a smear of roofs and masts and one white church tower.

My uncle came up from the galley with two mugs of tea and stood beside me without speaking, which was his way of saying that he was sorry for the argument and glad that I had come, and we drank while the land shrank and the swell began to lift us and drop us, lift us and drop us, in the long breathing motion of open water. Later I would learn the names of the men, the order of the watches, the small politics of the mess, the exact place where the hull groaned when the sea came from the northwest, but on that first morning I knew nothing except the cold and the noise and the enormous unsteady light.

The letter stayed in the bag for another three weeks. When I finally opened it, somewhere off the northern banks with the deck tilting under me and the crew asleep, it said only that she was proud, that the weather at home had been fine, that the garden had come in early, and that I should write when I could. I read it four times and then folded it back into its envelope, and I have carried it with me ever since, through ports and winters and jobs and years, because it is the only page I own that was written before any of this began. That was thirty years ago, and the harbour has been rebuilt twice, and the trawler was scrapped in a yard in Portugal, and my uncle has been dead for a decade, but the letter is still here.
